Regarding art in general I don't think you should base any determination on online/prints. I've seen a number of things a zillion times in that format and never cared for them, but when I saw them for real my opinion changed entirely. These are works that are meant to be viewed in person - sculptures, paintings, etc, are physical objects. A photo is a reproduction that can recall it but can never capture its spirit. Just do a quick image search for a painting by name and you'll notice that nearly every photo result has a different look! The effect in real life versus a photo viewed on a computer screen or even in print in most cases is even greater.

This is one reason I highly recommend visiting the best museums in great cities where they have this stuff. You can view it with your own eyes and see why these things are so well regarded. In my experience most well-regarded artists do have great work but often it's not the ones that are most famous. That's a product of people doing what OP said - pretending to like it because people say it's good.

A specific example I'll site - I live in NYC and at the MoMa they have the famous Starry Night by Van Gogh. There are always of course a gaggle of people looking at it and it's a big attraction. You've seen it in many forms throughout your life - coffee cups, bookmarks, placemats, everywhere. In real life it's not that exciting - it looks very much like all of those reproductions, is small, and generally underwhelming. It's not bad, but it's not amazing and doesn't jump out at you. All told I'd say it's more interesting for its content than its execution which is probably why the image is famous and works well in many forms but the painting itself is not so exciting. Meanwhile, in the same room is another Van Gogh that is not nearly as famous and which most museum visitors typically ignore:

https://img.encore-editions.com/big-archival-canvas-22451-22848-fm400.jpg

This is a terrific, fantastic, and evocative painting. If I'd only ever seen Starry Night I wouldn't be that impressed with Van Gogh and would feel similar to the OP regarding this famous artist. But I have seen this "Portrait of Joseph Roulin" and it is though I've met Mr. Roulin or even known him forever the painting so strongly captures a presence and personality. Would you ever know that from looking at the photos? Probably not.

This has been repeated on a dozen occasions and I no longer make any strong judgment on art or an artist without having seen the work in person.
